correctness.rationale: Writing n=m p^a with p the largest prime and p not dividing m gives R(n)=[1+(1+S(m))/(p-1)]/[p^(a-1) phi(m)]. The bound (2+omega(m))/phi(m) tends to zero by phi(m)>=sqrt(m/2), so a fixed threshold bounds m, and a>=2 then yields only finitely many possibilities. For fixed m and a=1, convergence to 1/phi(m) is strictly from above; this proves the weak multiplier cutoff even at equality. Multiple representations with distinct bounded m cause only finite corrections. For the first moment, summing over exact prime valuations gives coefficient p^(1-a)/phi(m); the terms a>=2 are O(sqrt(x)), the removed coprimality restriction for a=1 costs O(sqrt(x) log(x)), and the m>sqrt(x) tail is O(x^(3/4)). For smaller m the PNT bound permits summable domination after scaling by log(x)/x. For higher moments, the finitely many disjoint small-m families give their stated coefficients, and the complement is bounded by 2^(k-1) times its first-moment mass. The needed R<=2 also follows elementarily: the product of two or more odd-prime factors p-1 (each at least 2) is at least their sum; the smaller support cases give the same bound directly. Multiplicativity gives the displayed convergent Euler factors. Independent gcd-count and prime-family enumeration through 1600 reproduced H(1)=3/2 and H(1/2)=9/4 with finite count corrections -1 and -3 respectively, including the strict endpoint test. The proof, not the finite checks, supports the asymptotics.
residual_risks: The finite replay does not test the infinite prime-counting or moment limits. The result fixes t and k before x grows.

value.rationale: For a previously posed normalized-distribution problem this gives structure beyond typical convergence: it identifies essentially every positive-threshold exception and quantifies its density and contribution to all fixed integral moments. In particular the equality threshold is accounted for by a one-sided correction rather than being inferred from a limiting atom.
